subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: How fast? The rate of chemical change
themeLabel: How much, how fast and how far?
bigPicture: Rate is how fast concentration changes. Particles must collide with enough energy (at least Ea) and the right orientation, so anything that increases the number of successful collisions per second (concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature, a catalyst) speeds the reaction up. At HL you also measure exactly how rate depends on concentration and temperature, and use that to test mechanisms.

keyIdeas.cue: How is rate defined and measured?
keyIdeas.answer: Rate = change in concentration (or mass, volume) of a reactant or product per unit time, e.g. mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. From a concentration–time graph, the rate at any moment is the gradient of the tangent; the initial rate is the tangent at t = 0. Methods: gas volume, mass loss, colour (colorimeter), conductivity, time to a fixed point.
Particles react only if they collide with energy ≥ Ea and with a suitable orientation (geometry). Higher absolute temperature means higher average kinetic energy.

Higher concentration or gas pressure → more frequent collisions. Larger surface area (powder) → more collisions at the surface. Higher temperature → more frequent collisions and, much more importantly, a larger fraction with E ≥ Ea. Catalyst → lower Ea pathway.

keyIdeas.cue: What does a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution show?
keyIdeas.answer: Number of particles against kinetic energy; starts at the origin, has a peak, and a long tail that never touches the x-axis. Area under the curve = total number of particles. At higher T the peak moves right and lower, area unchanged, and the area beyond Ea grows a lot.

They provide an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so a larger fraction of collisions succeed; they are not used up and do not change ΔH or the position of equilibrium. Draw both energy profiles (catalysed hump lower) and mark the lower Ea on the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

keyIdeas.cue: What is a reaction mechanism and the rate-determining step (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: A sequence of elementary steps adding up to the overall equation. The slowest step decides the rate (rate-determining step, RDS); it need not be the first step. Intermediates are formed in one step and used in a later one (they sit in the energy 'valleys'); transition states are the unstable peaks. A valid mechanism must agree with the stoichiometry and the rate equation.

keyIdeas.cue: How do energy profiles show a multistep reaction (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: One hump per step; the highest-Ea hump is the rate-determining step; intermediates sit in the dips between humps.
Number of particles reacting in one elementary step: unimolecular (1), bimolecular (2), termolecular (3, rare).

keyIdeas.cue: How are rate equations and orders found (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, found only by experiment. From initial-rate data: double [A] with [B] fixed; rate ×1 → order 0, ×2 → 1, ×4 → 2. Overall order = m + n. Graphs: concentration–time is a straight downward line for zero order, a curve with constant half-life for first order, a steeper curve for second order. Rate–concentration: horizontal line (0), straight line through origin (1), upward curve (2). The orders show which species (and how many) are in the RDS.

keyIdeas.cue: What are the units of k (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Work them out from rate = k × concentrations: zero order mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; first order s⁻¹; second order dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; third order dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹. k rises with temperature.

keyIdeas.cue: How does the Arrhenius equation give Ea and A (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: k = A e^(−Ea/RT); linear form ln k = −Ea/(RT) + ln A. Plot ln k against 1/T: gradient = −Ea/R (so Ea = −gradient × 8.31, in J mol⁻¹) and y-intercept = ln A. A (the Arrhenius factor) represents how often collisions happen with the correct orientation.

keyTerms.def: Change in concentration per unit time.
Minimum energy colliding particles need to react.
Increases rate via a lower-Ea pathway; unchanged at the end.
Species formed then used up within a mechanism (AHL).
Power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation (AHL).
Proportionality constant in the rate equation; depends on temperature (AHL).
Frequency factor reflecting collisions with correct orientation (AHL).

workedExamples.title: Orders from initial rates (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: Exp 1: [A] 0.10, [B] 0.10, rate 2.0 × 10⁻³. Exp 2: [A] 0.20, [B] 0.10, rate 8.0 × 10⁻³. Exp 3: [A] 0.10, [B] 0.20, rate 2.0 × 10⁻³ (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹). Find the rate equation and k.
steps: A doubled, rate ×4: second order in A.
B doubled, rate unchanged: zero order in B.
workedExamples.answer: rate = k[A]²; k = 0.20 dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹

workedExamples.title: Ea from an Arrhenius plot (AHL)
workedExamples.prompt: A plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −6.00 × 10³ K. Calculate Ea.

misconceptions.wrong: Raising temperature speeds reactions mainly because particles collide more often.
misconceptions.right: The main effect is the much larger fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea.

misconceptions.wrong: A catalyst shifts the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve.
misconceptions.right: The curve is unchanged; the Ea line moves left so more particles exceed it.

misconceptions.wrong: Orders come from the balanced equation's coefficients.
misconceptions.right: Orders are found experimentally; they match coefficients only for the RDS of an elementary step.

practice.prompt: Explain, using a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, why a 10 K rise in temperature can roughly double the rate.
checkpoints: Curve at higher T: peak lower and moved right, same area
Many more particles have E ≥ Ea (area beyond Ea larger)
So the frequency of successful collisions increases greatly

paper1A.stem: Why does a powder react faster than a lump of the same mass?
Rate = k[X][Y]². What happens to the rate if both [X] and [Y] double?
Which units are correct for k in rate = k[A]?

paper1B.data: Volume of CO₂ from marble chips + HCl: t/s 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150; V/cm³ 0, 28, 46, 57, 62, 62.
paper1B.prompt: Describe how the rate changes and explain why it stops; estimate the average rate in the first 30 s.
paper1B.answer: Rate decreases as acid is used up (fewer collisions per second) and stops when the limiting reactant is gone (at about 120 s). Average rate over the first 30 s ≈ 28/30 = 0.93 cm³ s⁻¹.

paper1B.data: ln k against 1/T data: 1/T = 3.30 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −5.0; 1/T = 3.10 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −3.8.

assessmentNote: Paper 1A = multiple choice, no calculator; Paper 1B = data-based questions (format from public sources, confirm with the official guide). All prompts here are original practice, not predictions of exam questions.

errorHints.hint: On Maxwell–Boltzmann sketches keep the area the same and never let the curve touch the x-axis.
Arrhenius: Ea comes out in J mol⁻¹; divide by 1000 for kJ, and keep the gradient's sign straight.
Use the linear Arrhenius form from the booklet; don't rearrange from memory.
For temperature effects say 'greater proportion of collisions with E ≥ Ea', not just 'more energy'.
